Effects of hydrogen bond acceptor with benzyl group in deep eutectic solvents on pretreatment performance of bamboo residue

ARTICLE INFO --- Keywords: Bamboo residues Deep eutectic solvent Hydrogen bond acceptor Enzymatic hydrolysis Regenerated lignin

ABSTRACT Nine benzylammonium chloride-based deep eutectic solvents (DESs) were prepared and used to disrupt the natural recalcitrance of bamboo cell walls, to simultaneously produce fermentable sugars and lignin by-products. Under pretreatment conditions of 130 °C and 6 h, nearly 90% of lignin was removed during the tributyl benzyl ammonium chloride/oxalic acid (TBBAC/OA) pretreatment of Dendrocalamus giganteus Munro bamboo (DG), accompanied by a satisfactory recovery of cellulose (~84%). The enzymatic digestibility of TBBAC/OA-DG released 83.72% of fermentable sugars, which is about twice as high as tetrabutylammonium chloride/oxalic acid pretreated DG (TBAC/OA-DG) without benzyl groups as the hydrogen bond acceptor in the DES system. The structural characteristics of hydrogen bond acceptors (HBA) in DESs remarkably influenced the removal of lignin and xylan, which resulted in a loose structure after DES pretreatment, then increased the enzymatic accessibility of bamboo. Furthermore, the obtained regenerated lignin has a narrow molecular weight distribution and excellent solubility in organic solvents, which demonstrated potential industrial applications. These findings not only explain the relationship between HBA structure and bamboo fractionation, but also provide new insights for the selection and design of DES in biomass pretreatment.

1. Introduction Bamboo has fast growth cycle, high production rate and hol- ocellulose content, and is expected to become a promising substitute for wood resources during the biorefinery processing [1]. Dendrocalamus giganteus Munro (_D. giganteus_) bamboo extensively distributed in south- west of China were often used in the production of construction and other daily commodities. It is estimated that the utilization of these bamboo is only about 30%, while the annual processing waste is as high as 20 million tons [2,3]. The production of value-added compounds (sugar-based compounds and bioethanol) from bamboo residues have

attracted more attention for the development of bamboo biorefinery [4–7]. However, due to the high degree of lignification, high vascular bundles density, and complex cell wall structure of bamboo, efficient enzymatic saccharification has always been one of the main obstacles and expensive processes [8,9]. Therefore, biomass pretreatment has become an essential step towards high conversion of polysaccharide fraction as it can break the recalcitrance of biomass, and improve its accessibility to cellulase.

The green pretreatment technology of biomass has always been a research hotspot for the sustainable development of biorefinery in- dustry. In addition to achieving ideal pretreatment efficiency, it requires

the use of fewer toxic and harmful chemicals, the generation of fewer fermentation inhibitors, and the maximum biomass utilization [10]. During the developed pretreatment technologies, deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have become a promising method due to its low price, easy preparation, low toxicity and high biodegradability [11]. DESs are formed through mixing hydrogen bond donors (HBD) and hydrogen bond acceptors (HBA) in a specific molar ratio under heating conditions. HBD and HBA self-associated by means of hydrogen bond interactions, forming a homogeneous eutectic mixture with a melting point much lower than that of its individual component [12,13]. DES pretreatment has been proven to be effective in disrupting the cell wall structure of biomass, fractionating lignocellulose and increasing enzyme accessi- bility to cellulose substrates. There have been many reports on the ef- fects of HBDs (such as organic acids, amino acids, and sugars) on DES pretreatment of biomass, and it has been found that the design of HBDs was highly correlated with the selective extraction of lignin from lignocellulosic biomass [14]. However, little attention was paid to whether the HBA structure affected the DES characteristics and biomass pretreatment.

Hydrogen bond acceptors (HBAs) play a crucial role in the formation of DES and the number of hydrogen bonds in the system. Choline chloride (ChCl) is commonly used as HBAs in the synthesis of DES, because it was highly biodegradable, non-toxic, and can form DES with a wider range of HBDs [15,16]. Recently, benzylammonium chloride as an HBA has received increasing attention in DES pretreatment of biomass, because it has the same positively charged ammonium moiety and chloride ions as ChCl [17–21]. It belongs to the aromatic quaternary ammonium salt and has better phase transfer catalytic ability compared to ChCl, which meant that the solubility of lignin in benzylammonium chloride-based DES may be stronger than in ChCl-based DES. Corn cob was pretreated with benzyltrimethylammonium chloride-lactic acid, removing 80.8 % of xylan and 63.4 % of lignin [17]. Xie et al. [19] found that DES pretreatment of benzyltrimethylammonium chloride/formic acid (BTMAC/FA) can remove 78.03 % of pine lignin at 140 °C and 2 h. Bamboo shoot shells using benzyl triethylammonium chloride (BTEAC), formic acid (FA) and water pretreatment were performed on enzymatic hydrolysis, 87.0 % of monosaccharides was achieved. They found that BTEAC-based DES showed good potential in biomass pretreatment, because compared to ChCl-based DES, it had effective delignification and similar costs [20]. Although DES pretreatment using benzylammonium chloride as HBA has achieved some progress in the fractionation of biomass, efforts are still undertaken to improve its sustainability and diversified development.

In this study, a series of benzylammonium chloride-based DES with oxalic acid as an HBD were prepared; their properties were measured and compared. Then the benzylammonium chloride-based DESs were applied to treat bamboo residues for subsequent bioconversion of polysaccharides and preparation of lignin by-products. The relationship between the structure of benzylammonium chloride and the pretreatment performance of DES was investigated. The physicochemical properties of DES pretreated samples were systematically studied, and the mechanism of DES pretreatment with different HBAs was explored. Finally, the regenerated lignin was further characterized to promote the DESs-based biorefinery industrialization.

## 2. Materials and methods ### 2.1. Materials and reagents The Dendrocalamus giganteus Munro bamboo (_D. giganteus, DG_), were obtained from Baoshan City (Yunnan Province, China). They were ground and screened to 40-60 mesh for pretreatment experiments. Cellulase CTec2 (200 FPU/mL) was provided by Sigma Aldrich in Shanghai (China). Oxalic acid (OA, ≥99.5 %), trimethyl benzyl ammonium chloride (TMBAC, ≥98 %), triethyl benzyl ammonium chloride (TEBAC, ≥98 %), tripropyl benzyl ammonium chloride (TPBAC, ≥98

%), tributyl benzyl ammonium chloride (TBBAC, ≥98%), tetraethyl ammonium chloride (TEAC, ≥98%), tributyl ammonium chlorine (ТВАС, ≥98%), choline chloride (ChCl, ≥98%), tetradecyl dimethyl benzyl ammonium chloride (TDBAC, ≥98%), benzyl dimethyl (2- hydroxyethyl) ammonium chloride ([BzCh] Cl, ≥98%), were purchased from Shanghai Macklin Biochemical Co., Ltd.

2.2. _DES pretreatment using different HBAs and the extraction of regenerated lignin_ Benzylammonium chloride and oxalic acid (OA) in a molar ratio of 1:1 was mixed using a mild heating stirring method until a clear liquid was obtained. Due to the high viscosity of TPBAC/OA-DES and its inability to stir, 15 % water was added to adjust its viscosity to approximately the same as TEBAC/OA-DES in this study. The Kamlet-Taft polarity parameters (π*, β and α) of DES were measured using dye indicator (N, N-dimethyl-4-nitroaniline, 4-nitroaniline and Nile red) [18,22].

The prepared DES was mixed with bamboo powder in a high tem-perature reactor at a ratio of solid and liquid (1:10) and 130 °C for 6 h. Then the obtained mixture was subjected to vacuum filtration; the solid residue was repeatedly washed with hot water. The washing solution and the pretreatment solution was mixed together; this liquid fraction was treated with a 1:3 (v/v) ethanol/water mixture as antisolvent and then evaporated in a rotary evaporator to obtain DES regenerated lignin. The DES pretreated bamboo was defined based on the name of HBD and different HBAs. For example, _D. giganteus_ treated with tetraethy-lammonium chloride (TEAC) and oxalic acid (OA) was designated as TEAC/OA-DG. The chemical compositions of untreated and treated DG were measured using the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) protocol [22]. Three repeated measurements were conducted on all samples. The delignification, hemicellulose loss, and cellulose re-covery of DG were determined according to the content of each component in the pretreated substrates, as described in our previous research [23–25].

2.3. Enzymatic saccharification of pretreated bamboo Enzymatic hydrolysis of untreated and treated DG was performed in sodium citrate buffer solution (50 mM, pH 4.8) in 50 mL enzymatic bottles at 5 % (w/v) substrate loading. The mixtures were incubated at 50 °C in a shaking incubator with 150 rpm for 72 h, and the dosage of cellulase CTec2 was 20 FPU/g-sample. The supernatant was withdrawn periodically and the amount of releasing reducing glucose was determined using HPLC (Agilent 1260, USA), with an Aminex HPX-87H column and 5 mM H2SO4 (flow rate of 0.6 mL/min) as the mobile phase. Another experiment, Tween 80 (150 mg/g substrate) was added for reducing the nonproducing adsorption between pretreated samples and cellulase, then further improving the glucose yield during the hydrolysis process. All hydrolytic reactions were performed in duplicates. Glucose yield from enzymatic hydrolysis of pretreated DG was calculated based on following formula:
Glucose yield % = Glucose in the supernatant / (initial Glucan in bamboo × 1.11) × 100% (1)

After reaching equilibrium, the separation of solid-liquid phase was carried out at 10000 rpm for 10 min, then the protein amount of the supernatants was determined by Bradford assay. ## 2.5. Analytical methods ### 2.5.1. Characterization of pretreated samples The hydrophobicity and cellulose accessibility of bamboo after the DES pretreatments can be obtained based on the adsorption methods of Rose Bengal and Direct Red. Polymerization degree of different samples was determined using the cupriethylene diamine method. Two replicate determinations were run for all samples. A Sigma 300 (Germany) scanning electron microscope (SEM) was used to analyze the surface morphology of samples. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was obtained on an Escalab 250Xi 201 spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc., US), and the elemental compositions and surface lignin concentration was estimated as previously described [25]. The crystallinity indexes (CrI) of substrates were determined with X-ray diffractometer (Ultima IV, Rigaku, Japan) from 5° to 40° at 8°/min of scanning speed, and was estimated according to the method of Thygesen et al. [26]. The total specific surface areas of pretreated sample were carried out on Micrometritics ASAP 2020 analyzer (USA).

2.5.2. Characterization of DES-regenerated lignins The Mn (number average) and Mw (weight average) molecular weights of DES-lignins were investigated using Gel permeation chromatography (GPC, Agilent 1260 Infinity II, USA). Detailed structural changes in lignin were acquired by NMR spectrometer (Bruker AVIII 600, Germany); the sample preparation and operation methods were based on previous studies [27].

2.6. Computational analysis All HBA, HBD and DES molecules were geometrically optimized at B3LPY/6-31+G** level using Gaussian16 software [28]. Then a single-point energy calculation was carried out at B3LYP/def2-TZVPP level, which was used to evaluate hydrogen-bond interaction energy between HBAs and HBDs by Formula 2. After single-point energy calculation, molecular wave function information was obtained and Multiwfn program was used to calculate the Molecular Polarity Index (MPI) of the DESs molecules by Formula 3 [29,30]. The MPI values characterized the polarity of the DESs system. ## 3. Results and discussion ### 3.1. Effect of benzylammonium chloride-based DES on component separation of bamboo biomass

A series of DESs were synthesized using nine ammonium chloride and oxalic acid (OA) to investigate the effect of HBAs on the pretreat- ment performance of D. giganteus. The changes in chemical composition of DG after these DES pretreatments were shown in Fig. 1. As seen in Fig. 1, raw DG comprised 47.42 % cellulose, 16.61 % xylan, and 28.31 % lignin. All tested DES pretreatments resulted in a decrease of solid yield, indicating the dissolution of some chemical components in bamboo. Among the nine DESs, ChCl/OA provided the highest solid recovery (61.57 %), meant that its separation effect of bamboo cell wall compo- nents was not as good as other DES pretreatments. All DES pre- treatments, including ChCl/OA, exhibited significant removal of xylan, over 96 %, mainly due to the low stability of hemicellulose during acidic DES pretreatment under high temperature conditions. The free protons (H+) in acidic environment can catalyze and cleave ester and ether bonds between lignin and xylan, thereby separating and extracting amorphous structures of hemicellulose [33].

It was found that there was a clear correlation between the lignin removal and the structures of HBAs in DES system. As for DES pre- treatments with benzylammonium chloride as HBA, including TMBAC/ OA, TEBAC/OA, TPBAC/OA, TBBAC/OA, TDBAC/OA and [BzCh]Cl/ OA, the delignification was 76.76%, 83.06%, 92.08%, 88.36%, 74.06

This was attributed to the strong hydrogen bond formed between the chloride ions in HBA and the hy- droxyl groups in the solute, which is beneficial for the solubilization of lignin [34,35]. When the length of the alkyl chain increased, the delignification of DES pretreatment shows a trend of first increase and then gradually decrease, with TPBAC/OA and TBBAC/OA pretreatment having the higher delignification (92.08 % and 88.36 %). It was inter- esting that although the carbon chain structure of TBBAC was longer than that of TPBAC, the removal of lignin by TBBAC/OA was slightly lower than that of TPBAC/OA. Subsequently, TDBAC were also selected as HBA to analyze the effect of longer carbon chain on the delignifica- tion. It was observed no significant difference in the removal of lignin (76.76 % of TMBAC and 74.06 % of TDBAC), suggesting that the stronger steric hindrance to some extent hindered the removal of lignin. Meanwhile, compared with TMBAC and TDBAC, these HBAs (such as ChCl, TEAC and TBAC) lacked benzyl groups in their structures. The delignification decreased to 10.29 %, 70.89 %, and 75.79 %, respec- tively, implying that the benzyl structure of HBA could play an impor- tant role during the DES pretreatment of bamboo biomass. In comparison, a relatively poor delignification ability (10.29 %) was observed from the pretreatment of ChCl/OA. The structure of choline chloride contains hydroxyl groups, while [BzCh]Cl as HBA contained both benzyl and hydroxyl groups. It was observed that the delignifica- tion of [BzCh]Cl/OA increased to 72.85 %, which is about 7 times higher than that of ChCl/OA, suggesting that benzyl structure of HBAs demonstrated great effects on bamboo deconstruction. It was obvious that the HBA containing only benzyl group in the DESs had the best dissolving effect on lignin, followed by HBAs with both benzyl and hy- droxyl groups, and HBA with only hydroxyl groups has poor delignifi- cation. In addition, it can be seen that lignin and xylan were dissolved during the DES pretreatment process, while the solubility of these DES to cellulose was poor. The pretreated residue had a cellulose retention ratio of 74.06–83.78 %. The large number of intermolecular and intra- molecular hydrogen bonds in the cellulose structure made it difficult to
dissolve in DES.

As is well known, the delignification of DESs with quaternary ammonium cations as HBA depended on the ability of negative halogen anions to form lignin-chloride intermediates, which can affect the proton catalyzed depolymerization of lignin [14]. All tested HBAs are ammonium chloride, and its chloride ions can form strong hydrogen bonds with lignin, promoting the stretching and breaking of LCC structure and resulting in the dissolution of lignin. However, HBAs containing benzyl groups exhibited stronger ability of lignin removal, while the presence of hydroxyl groups in HBA had a negative effect on delignification. TMBAC, TEBАС, ТРВАС, ТBBAC, TDBAC and [BzCh]Cl belong to quaternary ammonium salts with aromatic ring, and their phase transfer catalytic ability are stronger than that of non-aromatic quaternary ammonium salts, which can improve the lignin solubility in the DESs [18]. Combined with the effect of free protons (H+) in acidic DES, the depolymerization of lignin was accelerated, effectively separating lignin in bamboo biomass. Benzyltrimethylammonium chloride/formic acid removed 78.03% of pine lignin at 140 °C for 2 h [19]. Triethylbenzylammonium chloride (TEBAC) is an aromatic ring quaternary ammonium salt. Liu et al. [18] found that when wheat straw (WS) was treated with DES of TEBAC/lactic acid, 79.73% of lignin was removed, and 91.27% of hydrolysis yield was achieved using cellulase of 35 FPU and β-glucosidase of 82 CBU.

## 3.2. Enzymatic saccharification of the pretreated bamboo residues After treating DG with DESs, the obtained solid residues were hydrolyzed with enzyme of 20 FPU/g sample. As shown in Fig. 2, the 72 h hydrolysis yield of raw DG were only 7.86 %. By comparison, it can be found that the enzymatic saccharification efficiency of bamboo wasters can be significantly enhanced after the benzylammonium chloride-based DES pretreatment. Among them, the TBBAC/OA pretreatment brought the higher glucose yield (83.72 %), while TPBAC/OA, TEBAC/OA, and TMBAC/OA pretreated DG gave 74.42 %, 65.18 % and 60.36 % glucose yield, respectively. It suggested that with the extension of HBA

carbon chain in the benzylammonium chloride-based DES, the enzymatic hydrolysis yield of pretreated substrates showed an increasing trend. The glucose yield of TBBAC/OA-DG increased by 38.7% compared to that of TMBAC/OA. This phenomenon may be due to the decrease of lignin content in TBBAC/OA-DG. As previously stated, the formation of strong hydrogen bonds between chloride ions and lignin, as well as the presence of aromatic ring structures in HBAs, contributed to the significant removal of lignin, which increased the exposure of carbohydrate in the pretreated substrates and improved the subsequent enzymatic hydrolysis yield. Moreover, it was found that glucose production was not entirely correlated with the above delignification. Although TPBAC/OA pretreatment resulted in the highest delignification (92.08 %), the hydrolysis yield was a little lower than that of TBBAC/OA. This was mainly because that except for the content of lignin, there were other factors that affected the enzymatic saccharification yield. It meant that the structure of TPBAC/OA-DG, such as the crystallinity, degree of polymerization, specific surface area, and hydrophilic/hydrophobic properties, is not beneficial for its enzymatic saccharification. A lower glucose yield of TDBAC (17.99%) was also observed, which is caused by the excessively long carbon chain of HBA due to its stronger steric hindrance.

As shown in Fig. 2a, the enzymatic hydrolysis efficiency of DG pretreated with benzylammonium chloride-based DES was significantly better than that of substrates lacking benzyl in HBAs. The cellulose conversion rate of TBAC/OA pretreated DG was 44.04 %, followed by TEAC/OA (34.08 %) and ChCl/OA (9 %) pretreatments, which were also correlated with the carbon chain length of HBA to a certain extent. The enzymatic hydrolysis yield of [BzCh]Cl/OA improved by about 4-folds than that of ChCl/OA, due to the introduction of benzyl structure. Compared with a non-aromatic ring HBA, benzylammonium chloride-based DES pretreatment showed a higher delignification (88.36 %), and correspondingly, the hydrolysis yield of pretreated DG increased by 2–4 times. The similar correlation between the benzyl structure of HBAs and the pretreatment performance was also observed in the initial enzymatic digestibility rate (Fig. 2b). The initial rate (within 6 h) of four pretreated substrates (TMBAC/OA-DG, TEBAC/OA-DG, TPBAC/OA-DG and TBBAC/OA-DG) were 0.37, 0.47, 0.55 and 0.59 g/L/h, respectively, which were about 2 times higher than TEAC/OA-DG and TBAC/OA-DG. The initial rate values of ChCl/OA-DG (0.044 g/L/h) were lower than that of [BzCh]Cl/OA-DG (0.199 g/L/h), indicating that the presence of benzyl groups in the HBA structure was beneficial for bamboo pretreatment. The higher initial rates in benzylammonium chloride-based DES pretreated samples may be related to the lower lignin content and substrate characteristics. The DES pretreatment containing benzyl groups in HBA has been used in the pretreatment process of various biomass, and the satisfactory performance has been achieved compared to DES pretreatment at the absence of benzyl groups in HBA. Zhang and coworkers have demonstrated that the DES of benzyltriethylammonium chloride (BTEAC) and formic acid (FA) can deconstruct the eucalyptus chips within 2 h at 130 °C, obtaining pure cellulose fibers [36]. Benzyltrimethylammonium chloride (BTMAC)/lactic acid (LA) pretreatment can remove 80.8 % of xylan and 63.4 % of lignin under 140 °C and 2 h, leading to 94.0 % of sugar yield under the enzyme usage of 15 FPU/g sample [17]. The DES of benzyltriethylammonium chloride and thymol has a better efficiency in extracting food dyes than the DES of choline chloride and thymol [37]. This was mainly because aromatic quaternary ammonium salts have stronger phase transfer capability, which can be dissolved in water and organic solvents. The negative and positive ions in quaternary ammonium salts formed an ion pair in the aqueous phase, which can transfer negative ions from the aqueous phase to the organic phase, while in the organic phase, negative ions have no solventization role [17,18].

This suggested that most of S-type units preferentially participate in the formation of β-O-4 linkage in this lignin, therefore only a small amount of free S-type OH group were found in the ³¹P NMR spectra. As seen in Table 3, after DES pretreatment, the amount of aliphatic hydroxyl groups decreased, while the amount of total phenolic hydroxyl groups significantly increased, from 0.75 mmol/g to 2.9–3.5 mmol/g. The increase in phenolic OH content was mainly due to the breaking of β-O-4 ether bonds in lignins; The reduction of aliphatic OH was attributed to dehydration and acylation reactions during the pretreatment. In addition, Table 3 also shows a significant increase in the content of non-condensed S-OH and G-OH groups, especially non-condensed S-OH groups. This fact indicated that in the DES system, the β-O-4 ether linkage was very easily dissociated. The increase in the number of S-type and G-OH groups in the condensation indicates that DES pretreatment can lead to the condensation reaction of lignin. Meanwhile, it was observed that the condensed-OH content of ChCl/OA-lignin (0.74 mmol/g) was significantly higher than that of TEBAC/OA-lignin (0.62 mmol/g) and TBBAC/OA-lignin (0.58 mmol/g), which may provide evidence for the high-level occurrence of lignin condensation during ChCl/OA pretreatment. TBBAC/OA pretreatment can significantly hinder the condensation reaction of lignin. Besides, the S/G ratio of lignin can also reflect the changes of structure occur during the processing. In Table 1, the S/G ratio of MWL was 0.36, lower than the values for ChCl/OA-lignin (0.86), TEBAC/OA-lignin (0.99) and TBBAC/OA-lignin (1.05). The increase of S/G ratio was explained by the fact that DES pretreatment was conducive to the preferential dissolution of S units from the cell wall and the easier condensation of G lignin units.

## 4. Conclusions This work demonstrated that the benzylammonium chloride-based DES pretreatment can achieve the efficient fractionation and bioconversion of bamboo biomass due to its better delignification and phase transfer catalytic ability. The removal of xylan and lignin was significantly improved to 96.86 % and 88.36 % under the optimal conditions with TBBAC/OA system at 130 °C for 6 h. Meanwhile, 83.72 % of enzymatic efficiency has been achieved by TBBAC/OA pretreatment, increased by 2–4 times than DES pretreatment with non-aromatic ring HBA. Moreover, DES-lignin had several unique features, including high purity, narrower molecular weight distribution and good solubility in many organic solvents. Therefore, this study provides a potential method for green and efficient fractionation and saccharification of bamboo cell wall components.

Under pretreatment conditions of 130 °C and 6 h, nearly 90% of lignin was removed during the tributyl benzyl ammonium chloride/oxalic acid (TBBAC/OA) pretreatment of Dendrocalamus giganteus Munro bamboo (DG), accompanied by a satisfactory recovery of cellulose (~84%). The enzymatic digestibility of TBBAC/OA-DG released 83.72% of fermentable sugars, which is about twice as high as tetrabutylammonium chloride/oxalic acid pretreated DG (TBAC/OA-DG) without benzyl groups as the hydrogen bond acceptor in the DES system. The structural characteristics of hydrogen bond acceptors (HBA) in DESs remarkably influenced the removal of lignin and xylan, which resulted in a loose structure after DES pretreatment, then increased the enzymatic accessibility of bamboo. Furthermore, the obtained regenerated lignin has a narrow molecular weight distribution and excellent solubility in organic solvents, which demonstrated potential industrial applications. These findings not only explain the relationship between HBA structure and bamboo fractionation, but also provide new insights for the selection and design of DES in biomass pretreatment. 1. Introduction Bamboo has fast growth cycle, high production rate and hol- ocellulose content, and is expected to become a promising substitute for wood resources during the biorefinery processing [1]. Dendrocalamus giganteus Munro (_D. giganteus_) bamboo extensively distributed in south- west of China were often used in the production of construction and other daily commodities. It is estimated that the utilization of these bamboo is only about 30%, while the annual processing waste is as high as 20 million tons [2,3]. The production of value-added compounds (sugar-based compounds and bioethanol) from bamboo residues have attracted more attention for the development of bamboo biorefinery [4–7]. However, due to the high degree of lignification, high vascular bundles density, and complex cell wall structure of bamboo, efficient enzymatic saccharification has always been one of the main obstacles and expensive processes [8,9]. Therefore, biomass pretreatment has become an essential step towards high conversion of polysaccharide fraction as it can break the recalcitrance of biomass, and improve its accessibility to cellulase. The green pretreatment technology of biomass has always been a research hotspot for the sustainable development of biorefinery in- dustry. During the developed pretreatment technologies, deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have become a promising method due to its low price, easy preparation, low toxicity and high biodegradability [11]. DESs are formed through mixing hydrogen bond donors (HBD) and hydrogen bond acceptors (HBA) in a specific molar ratio under heating conditions. HBD and HBA self-associated by means of hydrogen bond interactions, forming a homogeneous eutectic mixture with a melting point much lower than that of its individual component [12,13]. DES pretreatment has been proven to be effective in disrupting the cell wall structure of biomass, fractionating lignocellulose and increasing enzyme accessi- bility to cellulose substrates. There have been many reports on the ef- fects of HBDs (such as organic acids, amino acids, and sugars) on DES pretreatment of biomass, and it has been found that the design of HBDs was highly correlated with the selective extraction of lignin from lignocellulosic biomass [14]. However, little attention was paid to whether the HBA structure affected the DES characteristics and biomass pretreatment. Hydrogen bond acceptors (HBAs) play a crucial role in the formation of DES and the number of hydrogen bonds in the system. Choline chloride (ChCl) is commonly used as HBAs in the synthesis of DES, because it was highly biodegradable, non-toxic, and can form DES with a wider range of HBDs [15,16]. Recently, benzylammonium chloride as an HBA has received increasing attention in DES pretreatment of biomass, because it has the same positively charged ammonium moiety and chloride ions as ChCl [17–21]. It belongs to the aromatic quaternary ammonium salt and has better phase transfer catalytic ability compared to ChCl, which meant that the solubility of lignin in benzylammonium chloride-based DES may be stronger than in ChCl-based DES. Corn cob was pretreated with benzyltrimethylammonium chloride-lactic acid, removing 80.8 % of xylan and 63.4 % of lignin [17]. Xie et al. [19] found that DES pretreatment of benzyltrimethylammonium chloride/formic acid (BTMAC/FA) can remove 78.03 % of pine lignin at 140 °C and 2 h. Bamboo shoot shells using benzyl triethylammonium chloride (BTEAC), formic acid (FA) and water pretreatment were performed on enzymatic hydrolysis, 87.0 % of monosaccharides was achieved. They found that BTEAC-based DES showed good potential in biomass pretreatment, because compared to ChCl-based DES, it had effective delignification and similar costs [20]. Although DES pretreatment using benzylammonium chloride as HBA has achieved some progress in the fractionation of biomass, efforts are still undertaken to improve its sustainability and diversified development. In this study, a series of benzylammonium chloride-based DES with oxalic acid as an HBD were prepared; their properties were measured and compared. Then the benzylammonium chloride-based DESs were applied to treat bamboo residues for subsequent bioconversion of polysaccharides and preparation of lignin by-products. The relationship between the structure of benzylammonium chloride and the pretreatment performance of DES was investigated. The physicochemical properties of DES pretreated samples were systematically studied, and the mechanism of DES pretreatment with different HBAs was explored. Finally, the regenerated lignin was further characterized to promote the DESs-based biorefinery industrialization. ## 2. Materials and methods ### 2.1. Materials and reagents The Dendrocalamus giganteus Munro bamboo (_D. giganteus, DG_), were obtained from Baoshan City (Yunnan Province, China). They were ground and screened to 40-60 mesh for pretreatment experiments. Cellulase CTec2 (200 FPU/mL) was provided by Sigma Aldrich in Shanghai (China). Oxalic acid (OA, ≥99.5 %), trimethyl benzyl ammonium chloride (TMBAC, ≥98 %), triethyl benzyl ammonium chloride (TEBAC, ≥98 %), tripropyl benzyl ammonium chloride (TPBAC, ≥98 %), tributyl benzyl ammonium chloride (TBBAC, ≥98%), tetraethyl ammonium chloride (TEAC, ≥98%), tributyl ammonium chlorine (ТВАС, ≥98%), choline chloride (ChCl, ≥98%), tetradecyl dimethyl benzyl ammonium chloride (TDBAC, ≥98%), benzyl dimethyl (2- hydroxyethyl) ammonium chloride ([BzCh] Cl, ≥98%), were purchased from Shanghai Macklin Biochemical Co., Ltd. 2.2. _DES pretreatment using different HBAs and the extraction of regenerated lignin_ Benzylammonium chloride and oxalic acid (OA) in a molar ratio of 1:1 was mixed using a mild heating stirring method until a clear liquid was obtained. Due to the high viscosity of TPBAC/OA-DES and its inability to stir, 15 % water was added to adjust its viscosity to approximately the same as TEBAC/OA-DES in this study. The Kamlet-Taft polarity parameters (π*, β and α) of DES were measured using dye indicator (N, N-dimethyl-4-nitroaniline, 4-nitroaniline and Nile red) [18,22]. The prepared DES was mixed with bamboo powder in a high tem-perature reactor at a ratio of solid and liquid (1:10) and 130 °C for 6 h. Then the obtained mixture was subjected to vacuum filtration; the solid residue was repeatedly washed with hot water. The washing solution and the pretreatment solution was mixed together; this liquid fraction was treated with a 1:3 (v/v) ethanol/water mixture as antisolvent and then evaporated in a rotary evaporator to obtain DES regenerated lignin. The DES pretreated bamboo was defined based on the name of HBD and different HBAs. For example, _D. giganteus_ treated with tetraethy-lammonium chloride (TEAC) and oxalic acid (OA) was designated as TEAC/OA-DG. The chemical compositions of untreated and treated DG were measured using the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) protocol [22]. Three repeated measurements were conducted on all samples. The delignification, hemicellulose loss, and cellulose re-covery of DG were determined according to the content of each component in the pretreated substrates, as described in our previous research [23–25]. 2.3. Enzymatic saccharification of the pretreated bamboo residues After treating DG with DESs, the obtained solid residues were hydrolyzed with enzyme of 20 FPU/g sample. As shown in Fig. 2, the 72 h hydrolysis yield of raw DG were only 7.86 %. By comparison, it can be found that the enzymatic saccharification efficiency of bamboo wasters can be significantly enhanced after the benzylammonium chloride-based DES pretreatment. Among them, the TBBAC/OA pretreatment brought the higher glucose yield (83.72 %), while TPBAC/OA, TEBAC/OA, and TMBAC/OA pretreated DG gave 74.42 %, 65.18 % and 60.36 % glucose yield, respectively. It suggested that with the extension of HBA 4 Z. Liu et al. The glucose yield of TBBAC/OA-DG increased by 38.7% compared to that of TMBAC/OA. This phenomenon may be due to the decrease of lignin content in TBBAC/OA-DG. As previously stated, the formation of strong hydrogen bonds between chloride ions and lignin, as well as the presence of aromatic ring structures in HBAs, contributed to the significant removal of lignin, which increased the exposure of carbohydrate in the pretreated substrates and improved the subsequent enzymatic hydrolysis yield. Moreover, it was found that glucose production was not entirely correlated with the above delignification. Although TPBAC/OA pretreatment resulted in the highest delignification (92.08 %), the hydrolysis yield was a little lower than that of TBBAC/OA. This was mainly because that except for the content of lignin, there were other factors that affected the enzymatic saccharification yield. It meant that the structure of TPBAC/OA-DG, such as the crystallinity, degree of polymerization, specific surface area, and hydrophilic/hydrophobic properties, is not beneficial for its enzymatic saccharification. A lower glucose yield of TDBAC (17.99%) was also observed, which is caused by the excessively long carbon chain of HBA due to its stronger steric hindrance. As shown in Fig. 2a, the enzymatic hydrolysis efficiency of DG pretreated with benzylammonium chloride-based DES was significantly better than that of substrates lacking benzyl in HBAs. The cellulose conversion rate of TBAC/OA pretreated DG was 44.04 %, followed by TEAC/OA (34.08 %) and ChCl/OA (9 %) pretreatments, which were also correlated with the carbon chain length of HBA to a certain extent. The enzymatic hydrolysis yield of [BzCh]Cl/OA improved by about 4-folds than that of ChCl/OA, due to the introduction of benzyl structure. Compared with a non-aromatic ring HBA, benzylammonium chloride-based DES pretreatment showed a higher delignification (88.36 %), and correspondingly, the hydrolysis yield of pretreated DG increased by 2–4 times. The similar correlation between the benzyl structure of HBAs and the pretreatment performance was also observed in the initial enzymatic digestibility rate (Fig. 2b). The initial rate (within 6 h) of four pretreated substrates (TMBAC/OA-DG, TEBAC/OA-DG, TPBAC/OA-DG and TBBAC/OA-DG) were 0.37, 0.47, 0.55 and 0.59 g/L/h, respectively, which were about 2 times higher than TEAC/OA-DG and TBAC/OA-DG. The initial rate values of ChCl/OA-DG (0.044 g/L/h) were lower than that of [BzCh]Cl/OA-DG (0.199 g/L/h), indicating that the presence of benzyl groups in the HBA structure was beneficial for bamboo pretreatment. The higher initial rates in benzylammonium chloride-based DES pretreated samples may be related to the lower lignin content and substrate characteristics. The DES pretreatment containing benzyl groups in HBA has been used in the pretreatment process of various biomass, and the satisfactory performance has been achieved compared to DES pretreatment at the absence of benzyl groups in HBA. Zhang and coworkers have demonstrated that the DES of benzyltriethylammonium chloride (BTEAC) and formic acid (FA) can deconstruct the eucalyptus chips within 2 h at 130 °C, obtaining pure cellulose fibers [36]. The DES of benzyltriethylammonium chloride and thymol has a better efficiency in extracting food dyes than the DES of choline chloride and thymol [37]. This was mainly because aromatic quaternary ammonium salts have stronger phase transfer capability, which can be dissolved in water and organic solvents. The negative and positive ions in quaternary ammonium salts formed an ion pair in the aqueous phase, which can transfer negative ions from the aqueous phase to the organic phase, while in the organic phase, negative ions have no solventization role [17,18]. Cellulase adsorption isotherms on different DES pretreated D. giganteus To understand the impact of benzyl groups in HBA structure during the DES pretreatment on the enzymatic saccharification, the adsorption properties between cellulase and substrates were studied based on Langmuir adsorption isotherms (Fig. 3 and Table 1). As seen in Fig. 3, the enzymatic adsorption amount of raw DG was 33.98 mg protein/g- substrate. With the extension of carbon chains in benzyl HBAs struc- ture, the adsorption ability of cellulase on samples was significantly enhanced. The Γm values of cellulase on TMBAC/OA-DG, TEBAC/OA- DG, TPBAC/OA-DG and TBBAC/OA-DG were 59.6, 75.93, 86.82 and 83.6 mg/g, respectively, significantly higher than those of raw bamboo. Compared with TMBAC/OA-DG and TEBAC/OA-DG, TPBAC/OA and TBBAC/OA pretreated samples showed the higher cellulase adsorption capacity, which will also be beneficial for their subsequent enzymatic saccharification efficiency. In addition, the TDBAC/OA-DG has fewer binding sites to cellulase enzymes, as TDBAC is itself a cationic surfac- tant. Meanwhile, there are some differences in the Langmuir constant (K) and distribution coefficient (R) among all DES pretreated samples. The value of K and R improved to 14.57 mL/mg and 1.26 L/g-substrates for TPBAC/OA-DG, and 13.82 mL/mg and 1.16 L/g-substrates for TBBAC/OA-DG, indicating that the adsorption capacity of cellulase on substrates was significantly enhanced. This agreed well with the results of above enzyme hydrolysis, where TPBAC/OA-DG and TBBAC/OA-DG has the higher glucose production (74.42 % and 83.72 %). This was mainly due to DES pretreatment can destroy the complex structure of bamboo by removing most of hemicellulose and part of lignin, resulting in the increase of productive adsorption between cellulase and cellulose substrate [42]. Additionally, the cellulase adsorption activities is related to the physicochemical characteristics of sample. Conclusions This work demonstrated that the benzylammonium chloride-based DES pretreatment can achieve the efficient fractionation and bioconversion of bamboo biomass due to its better delignification and phase transfer catalytic ability. The removal of xylan and lignin was significantly improved to 96.86 % and 88.36 % under the optimal conditions with TBBAC/OA system at 130 °C for 6 h. Meanwhile, 83.72 % of enzymatic efficiency has been achieved by TBBAC/OA pretreatment, increased by 2–4 times than DES pretreatment with non-aromatic ring HBA. Moreover, DES-lignin had several unique features, including high purity, narrower molecular weight distribution and good solubility in many organic solvents. Therefore, this study provides a potential method for green and efficient fractionation and saccharification of bamboo cell wall components. Dendrocalamus giganteus Munro (_D. giganteus_) bamboo extensively distributed in south- west of China were often used in the production of construction and other daily commodities. It is estimated that the utilization of these bamboo is only about 30%, while the annual processing waste is as high as 20 million tons [2,3]. The production of value-added compounds (sugar-based compounds and bioethanol) from bamboo residues have attracted more attention for the development of bamboo biorefinery [4–7]. However, due to the high degree of lignification, high vascular bundles density, and complex cell wall structure of bamboo, efficient enzymatic saccharification has always been one of the main obstacles and expensive processes [8,9]. Therefore, biomass pretreatment has become an essential step towards high conversion of polysaccharide fraction as it can break the recalcitrance of biomass, and improve its accessibility to cellulase. During the developed pretreatment technologies, deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have become a promising method due to its low price, easy preparation, low toxicity and high biodegradability [11]. DESs are formed through mixing hydrogen bond donors (HBD) and hydrogen bond acceptors (HBA) in a specific molar ratio under heating conditions. HBD and HBA self-associated by means of hydrogen bond interactions, forming a homogeneous eutectic mixture with a melting point much lower than that of its individual component [12,13]. DES pretreatment has been proven to be effective in disrupting the cell wall structure of biomass, fractionating lignocellulose and increasing enzyme accessi- bility to cellulose substrates. There have been many reports on the ef- fects of HBDs (such as organic acids, amino acids, and sugars) on DES pretreatment of biomass, and it has been found that the design of HBDs was highly correlated with the selective extraction of lignin from lignocellulosic biomass [14]. However, little attention was paid to whether the HBA structure affected the DES characteristics and biomass pretreatment. Hydrogen bond acceptors (HBAs) play a crucial role in the formation of DES and the number of hydrogen bonds in the system. Choline chloride (ChCl) is commonly used as HBAs in the synthesis of DES, because it was highly biodegradable, non-toxic, and can form DES with a wider range of HBDs [15,16]. Recently, benzylammonium chloride as an HBA has received increasing attention in DES pretreatment of biomass, because it has the same positively charged ammonium moiety and chloride ions as ChCl [17–21]. It belongs to the aromatic quaternary ammonium salt and has better phase transfer catalytic ability compared to ChCl, which meant that the solubility of lignin in benzylammonium chloride-based DES may be stronger than in ChCl-based DES. Corn cob was pretreated with benzyltrimethylammonium chloride-lactic acid, removing 80.8 % of xylan and 63.4 % of lignin [17]. Xie et al. [19] found that DES pretreatment of benzyltrimethylammonium chloride/formic acid (BTMAC/FA) can remove 78.03 % of pine lignin at 140 °C and 2 h. Bamboo shoot shells using benzyl triethylammonium chloride (BTEAC), formic acid (FA) and water pretreatment were performed on enzymatic hydrolysis, 87.0 % of monosaccharides was achieved. They found that BTEAC-based DES showed good potential in biomass pretreatment, because compared to ChCl-based DES, it had effective delignification and similar costs [20]. Although DES pretreatment using benzylammonium chloride as HBA has achieved some progress in the fractionation of biomass, efforts are still undertaken to improve its sustainability and diversified development. In this study, a series of benzylammonium chloride-based DES with oxalic acid as an HBD were prepared; their properties were measured and compared. Then the benzylammonium chloride-based DESs were applied to treat bamboo residues for subsequent bioconversion of polysaccharides and preparation of lignin by-products. The relationship between the structure of benzylammonium chloride and the pretreatment performance of DES was investigated. The physicochemical properties of DES pretreated samples were systematically studied, and the mechanism of DES pretreatment with different HBAs was explored. Finally, the regenerated lignin was further characterized to promote the DESs-based biorefinery industrialization. ## 2. Materials and methods ### 2.1. Materials and reagents The Dendrocalamus giganteus Munro bamboo (_D. giganteus, DG_), were obtained from Baoshan City (Yunnan Province, China). They were ground and screened to 40-60 mesh for pretreatment experiments. Cellulase CTec2 (200 FPU/mL) was provided by Sigma Aldrich in Shanghai (China). Oxalic acid (OA, ≥99.5 %), trimethyl benzyl ammonium chloride (TMBAC, ≥98 %), triethyl benzyl ammonium chloride (TEBAC, ≥98 %), tripropyl benzyl ammonium chloride (TPBAC, ≥98 %), tributyl benzyl ammonium chloride (TBBAC, ≥98%), tetraethyl ammonium chloride (TEAC, ≥98%), tributyl ammonium chlorine (ТВАС, ≥98%), choline chloride (ChCl, ≥98%), tetradecyl dimethyl benzyl ammonium chloride (TDBAC, ≥98%), benzyl dimethyl (2- hydroxyethyl) ammonium chloride ([BzCh] Cl, ≥98%), were purchased from Shanghai Macklin Biochemical Co., Ltd. 2.2. _DES pretreatment using different HBAs and the extraction of regenerated lignin_ Benzylammonium chloride and oxalic acid (OA) in a molar ratio of 1:1 was mixed using a mild heating stirring method until a clear liquid was obtained. Due to the high viscosity of TPBAC/OA-DES and its inability to stir, 15 % water was added to adjust its viscosity to approximately the same as TEBAC/OA-DES in this study. The Kamlet-Taft polarity parameters (π*, β and α) of DES were measured using dye indicator (N, N-dimethyl-4-nitroaniline, 4-nitroaniline and Nile red) [18,22]. The prepared DES was mixed with bamboo powder in a high tem-perature reactor at a ratio of solid and liquid (1:10) and 130 °C for 6 h. Then the obtained mixture was subjected to vacuum filtration; the solid residue was repeatedly washed with hot water. The washing solution and the pretreatment solution was mixed together; this liquid fraction was treated with a 1:3 (v/v) ethanol/water mixture as antisolvent and then evaporated in a rotary evaporator to obtain DES regenerated lignin. The DES pretreated bamboo was defined based on the name of HBD and different HBAs. For example, _D. giganteus_ treated with tetraethy-lammonium chloride (TEAC) and oxalic acid (OA) was designated as TEAC/OA-DG. The structure of choline chloride contains hydroxyl groups, while [BzCh]Cl as HBA contained both benzyl and hydroxyl groups. It was observed that the delignifica- tion of [BzCh]Cl/OA increased to 72.85 %, which is about 7 times higher than that of ChCl/OA, suggesting that benzyl structure of HBAs demonstrated great effects on bamboo deconstruction. It was obvious that the HBA containing only benzyl group in the DESs had the best dissolving effect on lignin, followed by HBAs with both benzyl and hy- droxyl groups, and HBA with only hydroxyl groups has poor delignifi- cation. In addition, it can be seen that lignin and xylan were dissolved during the DES pretreatment process, while the solubility of these DES to cellulose was poor. The pretreated residue had a cellulose retention ratio of 74.06–83.78 %. The large number of intermolecular and intra- molecular hydrogen bonds in the cellulose structure made it difficult to dissolve in DES. As is well known, the delignification of DESs with quaternary ammonium cations as HBA depended on the ability of negative halogen anions to form lignin-chloride intermediates, which can affect the proton catalyzed depolymerization of lignin [14]. All tested HBAs are ammonium chloride, and its chloride ions can form strong hydrogen bonds with lignin, promoting the stretching and breaking of LCC structure and resulting in the dissolution of lignin. However, HBAs containing benzyl groups exhibited stronger ability of lignin removal, while the presence of hydroxyl groups in HBA had a negative effect on delignification. TMBAC, TEBАС, ТРВАС, ТBBAC, TDBAC and [BzCh]Cl belong to quaternary ammonium salts with aromatic ring, and their phase transfer catalytic ability are stronger than that of non-aromatic quaternary ammonium salts, which can improve the lignin solubility in the DESs [18]. Combined with the effect of free protons (H+) in acidic DES, the depolymerization of lignin was accelerated, effectively separating lignin in bamboo biomass. Benzyltrimethylammonium chloride/formic acid removed 78.03% of pine lignin at 140 °C for 2 h [19]. Triethylbenzylammonium chloride (TEBAC) is an aromatic ring quaternary ammonium salt. Liu et al. [18] found that when wheat straw (WS) was treated with DES of TEBAC/lactic acid, 79.73% of lignin was removed, and 91.27% of hydrolysis yield was achieved using cellulase of 35 FPU and β-glucosidase of 82 CBU. ## 3.2. Enzymatic saccharification of the pretreated bamboo residues After treating DG with DESs, the obtained solid residues were hydrolyzed with enzyme of 20 FPU/g sample. As shown in Fig. 2, the 72 h hydrolysis yield of raw DG were only 7.86 %. By comparison, it can be found that the enzymatic saccharification efficiency of bamboo wasters can be significantly enhanced after the benzylammonium chloride-based DES pretreatment. Among them, the TBBAC/OA pretreatment brought the higher glucose yield (83.72 %), while TPBAC/OA, TEBAC/OA, and TMBAC/OA pretreated DG gave 74.42 %, 65.18 % and 60.36 % glucose yield, respectively. It suggested that with the extension of HBA 4 Z. Liu et al. Renewable Energy 246 (2025) 122891 carbon chain in the benzylammonium chloride-based DES, the enzymatic hydrolysis yield of pretreated substrates showed an increasing trend. The glucose yield of TBBAC/OA-DG increased by 38.7% compared to that of TMBAC/OA. This phenomenon may be due to the decrease of lignin content in TBBAC/OA-DG. As previously stated, the formation of strong hydrogen bonds between chloride ions and lignin, as well as the presence of aromatic ring structures in HBAs, contributed to the significant removal of lignin, which increased the exposure of carbohydrate in the pretreated substrates and improved the subsequent enzymatic hydrolysis yield. Moreover, it was found that glucose production was not entirely correlated with the above delignification. Although TPBAC/OA pretreatment resulted in the highest delignification (92.08 %), the hydrolysis yield was a little lower than that of TBBAC/OA. This was mainly because that except for the content of lignin, there were other factors that affected the enzymatic saccharification yield. It meant that the structure of TPBAC/OA-DG, such as the crystallinity, degree of polymerization, specific surface area, and hydrophilic/hydrophobic properties, is not beneficial for its enzymatic saccharification. A lower glucose yield of TDBAC (17.99%) was also observed, which is caused by the excessively long carbon chain of HBA due to its stronger steric hindrance. As shown in Fig. 2a, the enzymatic hydrolysis efficiency of DG pretreated with benzylammonium chloride-based DES was significantly better than that of substrates lacking benzyl in HBAs. The cellulose conversion rate of TBAC/OA pretreated DG was 44.04 %, followed by TEAC/OA (34.08 %) and ChCl/OA (9 %) pretreatments, which were also correlated with the carbon chain length of HBA to a certain extent. The enzymatic hydrolysis yield of [BzCh]Cl/OA improved by about 4-folds than that of ChCl/OA, due to the introduction of benzyl structure. Compared with a non-aromatic ring HBA, benzylammonium chloride-based DES pretreatment showed a higher delignification (88.36 %), and correspondingly, the hydrolysis yield of pretreated DG increased by 2–4 times. The similar correlation between the benzyl structure of HBAs and the pretreatment performance was also observed in the initial enzymatic digestibility rate (Fig. 2b). The initial rate (within 6 h) of four pretreated substrates (TMBAC/OA-DG, TEBAC/OA-DG, TPBAC/OA-DG and TBBAC/OA-DG) were 0.37, 0.47, 0.55 and 0.59 g/L/h, respectively, which were about 2 times higher than TEAC/OA-DG and TBAC/OA-DG. The initial rate values of ChCl/OA-DG (0.044 g/L/h) were lower than that of [BzCh]Cl/OA-DG (0.199 g/L/h), indicating that the presence of benzyl groups in the HBA structure was beneficial for bamboo pretreatment. The higher initial rates in benzylammonium chloride-based DES pretreated samples may be related to the lower lignin content and substrate characteristics. The DES pretreatment containing benzyl groups in HBA has been used in the pretreatment process of various biomass, and the satisfactory performance has been achieved compared to DES pretreatment at the absence of benzyl groups in HBA. Zhang and coworkers have demonstrated that the DES of benzyltriethylammonium chloride (BTEAC) and formic acid (FA) can deconstruct the eucalyptus chips within 2 h at 130 °C, obtaining pure cellulose fibers [36]. Benzyltrimethylammonium chloride (BTMAC)/lactic acid (LA) pretreatment can remove 80.8 % of xylan and 63.4 % of lignin under 140 °C and 2 h, leading to 94.0 % of sugar yield under the enzyme usage of 15 FPU/g sample [17]. The DES of benzyltriethylammonium chloride and thymol has a better efficiency in extracting food dyes than the DES of choline chloride and thymol [37]. This was mainly because aromatic quaternary ammonium salts have stronger phase transfer capability, which can be dissolved in water and organic solvents. The negative and positive ions in quaternary ammonium salts formed an ion pair in the aqueous phase, which can transfer negative ions from the aqueous phase to the organic phase, while in the organic phase, negative ions have no solventization role [17,18]. Conclusions This work demonstrated that the benzylammonium chloride-based DES pretreatment can achieve the efficient fractionation and bioconversion of bamboo biomass due to its better delignification and phase transfer catalytic ability. The removal of xylan and lignin was significantly improved to 96.86 % and 88.36 % under the optimal conditions with TBBAC/OA system at 130 °C for 6 h. Meanwhile, 83.72 % of enzymatic efficiency has been achieved by TBBAC/OA pretreatment, increased by 2–4 times than DES pretreatment with non-aromatic ring HBA. Moreover, DES-lignin had several unique features, including high purity, narrower molecular weight distribution and good solubility in many organic solvents. Therefore, this study provides a potential method for green and efficient fractionation and saccharification of bamboo cell wall components.
